newsitem.title: USA: US High Court to hear credit union/bank dispute.
newsitem.headline: US High Court to hear credit union/bank dispute.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court said Monday it would decide whether federal regulators have properly allowed credit unions to expand their membership to unrelated companies or professions in different areas.
The case is a high-stakes dispute involving the banking industry, federal regulators and cooperative, non-profit credit unions that offer bank-like services.

The high court agreed to hear an appeal by the Justice Department on behalf of the federal regulatory agency, the National Credit Union Administration (NCUA), and by the AT&T Family Federal Credit Union of Winston-Salem, N.C.
The Supreme Court will hear arguments in the case in its upcoming term that begins in October. A decision is likely early next year.
Until 1982, credit unions were limited to having members with a single common bond -- people who worked for the same employer or lived in the same neighborhood.

But in 1982, concerned about looming financial problems for credit unions, the NCUA reinterpreted a 1934 law and allowed credit unions to diversify their memberships beyond single companies to other occupations and other areas.
The American Bankers Association trade group and five North Carolina banks sued in 1990 to challenge the NCUA approval of AT&T's credit union expansion.
Only about a third of AT&T Family Federal's members now actually work for the phone company. It has members in various states who work at a number of unrelated companies.
The banking industry has complained that the larger, tax-exempt credit unions pose unfair competition.
A federal judge ruled for the NCUA, but a federal appeals court last July held that the law requires that all members of a credit union share a single common bond.
Justice Department lawyer Walter Dellinger said in the Supreme Court appeal that the issue was of "extraordinary importance" to the 3,600 credit unions in the U.S.
Those credit unions serve 32 million people, have assets of $150 billion, have loans of $94 billion, and hold $132 billion on deposit, he said.
Dellinger said the appeals court ruling "threatens nationwide instability and losses in the credit union industry affecting millions of persons."
